claim: Sleep in Drosophila shares many features with sleep in humans.
source: Sleep in Drosophila shares many features with sleep in humans.
evidence: This is a general statement drawing from established scientific knowledge about Drosophila as a model organism for sleep research.

claim: Flies adjust their sleep behavior depending on other needs.
source: Like humans, flies adjust their sleep behavior depending on other needs (Griffith, 2013).
evidence: Supported by citation to Griffith, 2013.

claim: Starved flies sleep less than well-fed flies, presumably to forage for food.
source: Starved flies sleep less than well-fed flies, presumably to forage for food (Keene et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to Keene et al., 2010, with speculative reasoning about foraging.

claim: Female flies sleep less after mating, presumably to lay eggs.
source: female flies sleep less after mating, presumably to lay eggs (Isaac et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citation to Isaac et al., 2010, with speculative reasoning about egg laying.

claim: Mixed-sex groups of flies sleep less than single-sex groups, presumably to engage in sexual activities.
source: mixed-sex groups of flies sleep less than single-sex groups, presumably to engage in sexual activities (Liu et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Liu et al., 2015, with speculative reasoning about sexual activities.

claim: Norepinephrine and its Drosophila counterpart octopamine act as wake-promoting signals.
source: Earlier studies have shown that norepinephrine and its Drosophila counterpart octopamine act as wake-promoting signals (Aston-Jones and Bloom, 1981; Carter et al., 2010; Crocker and Sehgal, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Aston-Jones and Bloom, 1981; Carter et al., 2010; Crocker and Sehgal, 2008.

claim: Sleep amount was markedly reduced in MF pairs relative to MM pairs.
source: Sleep amount was markedly reduced in MF pairs relative to MM pairs (Figure 1A,B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A,B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: Isolated females exhibited reduced daytime sleep relative to isolated males.
source: As expected, isolated females exhibited reduced daytime sleep relative to isolated males
evidence: Supported by experimental data and consistent with prior expectations.

claim: The reduction in daytime sleep in isolated females was comparable to the daytime sleep reduction in MF relative to MM pairs.
source: the reduction was comparable to the daytime sleep reduction in MF relative to MM pairs (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The difference in daytime sleep between MF and MM pairs is largely due to female wakefulness.
source: consistent with the possibility that the difference in daytime sleep between MF and MM pairs is largely due to female wakefulness
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of sleep patterns between isolated flies and pairs.

claim: Nighttime sleep loss in MF relative to MM pairs is considerably greater than the difference in sleep amount between isolated males and females.
source: In contrast, nighttime sleep loss in MF relative to MM pairs is considerably greater than the difference in sleep amount between isolated males and females (Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The nighttime sleep loss in MF pairs is not simply due to the presence of another fly or sex differences in sleep amount between males and females in isolation.
source: which suggests that the nighttime sleep loss in MF pairs is not simply due to the presence of another fly or sex differences in sleep amount between males and females in isolation
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of nighttime sleep loss patterns.

claim: Males paired with females spent much of the night engaged in courtship.
source: To assess nighttime behavior of individual flies in MM or MF pairs, we made video recordings under infrared light, which revealed that males paired with females spent much of the night engaged in courtship (Video 1).
evidence: Supported by video recordings (Video 1).

claim: Individual male flies slept more in MM pairs than in MF pairs.
source: Individual male flies slept more in MM pairs than in MF pairs (Figure 1C)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Awake males spent most of their time courting in MF pairs.
source: with awake males spending most of their time courting in MF pairs (Figure 1D)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Males in MM pairs did not exhibit courtship behavior.
source: a behavior not exhibited by either male in MM pairs
evidence: Supported by experimental observations.

claim: Only ~2% of the time was a female awake while its male partner was asleep.
source: Pairs of flies tended to be awake or asleep together, and only ~2% of the time was a female awake while its male partner was asleep.
evidence: Supported by experimental data from video analysis.

claim: Sleep in a pair of flies (defined as when both flies are asleep) is a good measure of sleep in a single male fly in the pair.
source: As a result, sleep in a pair of flies (defined as when both flies are asleep) is a good measure of sleep in a single male fly in the pair (Figure 1C).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that flies tend to be awake or asleep together.

claim: Males spend much of the night courting instead of sleeping when paired with females.
source: These results demonstrate that males spend much of the night courting instead of sleeping when paired with females
evidence: Supported by experimental data from video analysis.

claim: Daily rhythms in the proximity between flies in MF pairs are driven by male sex drive.
source: Our data, together with previous work that employed video tracking to conclude that daily rhythms in the proximity between flies in MF pairs are driven by male sex drive (Fujii et al., 2007)
evidence: Supported by citation to Fujii et al., 2007.

claim: Male flies possess mechanisms for suppressing sleep in the presence of female flies.
source: led to the idea that male flies possess mechanisms for suppressing sleep in the presence of female flies
evidence: Inferred from experimental observations and previous work.

claim: Male flies housed with a number of virgin females exhibited reduced courtship and copulation behaviors over a ~5 hr period.
source: As previously shown, male flies housed with a number of virgin females exhibited reduced courtship and copulation behaviors over a ~5 hr period (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1.

claim: A satiated male that had been grouped with virgin females slept more than a naive male that had been grouped with other males when paired with a female in a DAM.
source: When paired with a female in a DAM, a satiated male that had been grouped with virgin females slept more than a naive male that had been grouped with other males (Figure 2A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Satiated males exhibited increased sleep accompanied by decreased courtship index.
source: Video analysis confirmed that satiated males exhibited increased sleep accompanied by decreased courtship index (Figure 2B,C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B,C.

claim: When sex drive is satisfied, the normal level of nighttime sleep drive is sufficient to allow males to sleep in the presence of females.
source: These data suggest that when sex drive is satisfied, the normal level of nighttime sleep drive is sufficient to allow males to sleep in the presence of females.
evidence: Inferred from the satiety experiment results.

claim: MF pairs slept as much as MM pairs following 6 hr of sleep deprivation.
source: Whereas MF pairs slept less than MM pairs under non-deprived conditions, MF pairs slept as much as MM pairs following 6 hr of sleep deprivation (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Sleep-deprived males slept more and courted less than non-deprived males.
source: Video analysis confirmed that sleep-deprived males slept more and courted less than non-deprived males (Figure 2E,F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E,F.

claim: Excessive sleep drive can overcome sex drive.
source: These results demonstrate that excessive sleep drive can overcome sex drive.
evidence: Inferred from the sleep deprivation experiment results.

claim: The dFSB is thought to function in the output arm of the sleep homeostat.
source: The dFSB is thought to function in the output arm of the sleep homeostat (Donlea et al., 2014, Donlea et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Donlea et al., 2014, Donlea et al., 2011.

claim: Activation of dFSB induced sleep in isolated males.
source: As expected, activation of dFSB induced sleep in isolated males (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Males with activated dFSB slept almost as much when paired with control females (MFc) as when paired with control males (MMc) at night.
source: Notably, males with activated dFSB slept almost as much when paired with control females (MFc) as when paired with control males (MMc) at night (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Parental controls exhibited the normal pattern of reduced nighttime sleep in MFc relative to MMc pairs.
source: In contrast, parental controls, i.e., males carrying either R23E10-Gal4 or UAS-NaChBac alone, exhibited the normal pattern of reduced nighttime sleep in MFc relative to MMc pairs (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2G.

claim: Elevated sleep drive suppresses sexual behavior.
source: These data provide further evidence that elevated sleep drive suppresses sexual behavior.
evidence: Inferred from the dFSB activation experiment results.

claim: The relative strength of sleep drive and sex drive determines whether a male engages in sleep or courtship.
source: Together, our data demonstrate that the relative strength of sleep drive and sex drive determines whether a male engages in sleep or courtship.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of satiety, sleep deprivation, and dFSB activation experiments.

claim: Activation of MS1 neurons led to decreased sleep in isolated males, but not in isolated females.
source: We found that activation of MS1 neurons led to decreased sleep in isolated males, but not in isolated females (Figure 3A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Males with activated MS1 neurons did not exhibit male-specific behaviors, such as courtship and aggression, but instead exhibited locomotor behavior typically observed in awake flies.
source: Males with activated MS1 neurons did not exhibit male-specific behaviors, such as courtship and aggression, but instead exhibited locomotor behavior typically observed in awake flies, i.e., pacing the perimeter of the recording arena (Video 2).
evidence: Supported by video observations (Video 2).

claim: Males with activated MS1 neurons lost about 2/3 of nighttime sleep relative to controls at 29°C.
source: Although males with activated MS1 neurons lost about 2/3 of nighttime sleep relative to controls at 29°C, they slept no more than the control males when the temperature was returned to 22°C (Figure 3A)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Sleep loss due to activated MS1 neurons does not lead to recovery sleep.
source: suggesting that sleep loss due to activated MS1 neurons does not lead to recovery sleep
evidence: Inferred from the observation that males did not sleep more after MS1 activation was stopped.

claim: MS1 neurons function in adult male flies to promote wakefulness.
source: Since the TrpA1 channels were activated for only one day during the adult stage, these results indicate that MS1 neurons function in adult male flies to promote wakefulness.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental design and results.

claim: Constitutive activation of MS1 neurons by NaChBac expression resulted in male-specific sleep reduction.
source: Constitutive activation of MS1 neurons by NaChBac expression also resulted in male-specific sleep reduction (Figure 3B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Both chronic and acute activation of MS1 neurons affect male sleep.
source: demonstrating that both chronic and acute activation of MS1 neurons affect male sleep
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of TrpA1 and NaChBac experiments.

claim: Silencing of MS1 neurons via TNT expression did not affect sleep in isolated males.
source: When we expressed tetanus toxin (TNT) in MS1 neurons to block neurotransmission, sleep in isolated males was not altered (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: MS1 neurons become activated only under specific social contexts.
source: We hypothesized this may be because MS1 neurons become activated only under specific social contexts.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the observation that silencing MS1 neurons did not affect sleep in isolated males.

claim: Silencing of MS1 neurons did not affect sleep in MMc pairs.
source: Indeed, whereas silencing of MS1 neurons via TNT expression did not affect sleep in MMc pairs (experimental males paired with control males)
evidence: Supported by experimental data.

claim: Silencing of MS1 neurons led to a significant occlusion of the nighttime sleep loss in MFc pairs.
source: it led to a significant occlusion of the nighttime sleep loss in MFc pairs (Figure 3C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Males with silenced MS1 neurons slept more and courted less than parental control males.
source: Males with silenced MS1 neurons slept more and courted less than parental control males (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D,E.

claim: Activation of MS1 neurons is dependent on female cues and is required to keep males awake in the presence of females.
source: These data suggest that activation of MS1 neurons is dependent on female cues and is required to keep males awake in the presence of females, presumably so that they can engage in sustained courtship.
evidence: Inferred from the experimental results with speculative reasoning about courtship.

claim: Inhibition of MS1 activity by TNT expression had little effect on courtship index and copulation latency when assayed under white light conditions.
source: Inhibition of MS1 activity by TNT expression had little effect on courtship index and copulation latency when assayed under white light conditions (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F,G.

claim: Inhibition of MS1 activity by TNT expression had little effect on courtship index but had a significant effect on copulation latency in infrared light during the subjective day.
source: We found that whereas inhibition of MS1 activity by TNT expression had little effect on courtship index, it had a significant effect on copulation latency (Figure 3F,G).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3F,G.

claim: MS1 neuronal activity is not directly required for copulation.
source: Since males with silenced MS1 neurons can successfully copulate in the light condition, it is unlikely that MS1 neuronal activity is directly required for copulation.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that males with silenced MS1 neurons can copulate in light.

claim: MS1 neuronal activity may be required for timely progression through stages of courtship in the dark.
source: Instead it may be required for timely progression through stages of courtship in the dark.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the copulation latency results.

claim: MS1>TNT males were less successful in mating when competing against control males.
source: Consistent with delayed copulation in these assays, MS1>TNT males were also less successful in mating when competing against control males (Figure 3H).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3H.

claim: MS1 neuronal activity is important for optimal mating performance in the dark, especially during the night when sleep drive is high.
source: Together, our findings suggest that MS1 neuronal activity is important for optimal mating performance in the dark, especially during the night when sleep drive is high.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of courtship and competitive mating assays.

claim: MS1-Gal4 shows a restricted pattern of expression in 3 to 7 neurons in the subesophageal ganglion (SOG) near the midline and ~4 pairs of neurons in the dorsal brain.
source: We next examined the expression pattern of MS1-Gal4 using membrane-bound GFP, and found a restricted pattern of expression in 3 to 7 neurons in the subesophageal ganglion (SOG) near the midline and ~4 pairs of neurons in the dorsal brain (Figure 4A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: No cell bodies were detectable in the ventral nerve cord, although there were descending projections from the central brain.
source: No cell bodies were detectable in the ventral nerve cord, although there were descending projections from the central brain (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Differences between male and female expression patterns of MS1-Gal4 were not apparent.
source: Differences between male and female expression patterns were not apparent.
evidence: Supported by experimental observations.

claim: Some of the projection patterns of the MS1 neurons in the SOG resemble those of octopaminergic neurons.
source: We noticed that some of the projection patterns of the MS1 neurons in the SOG resemble those of octopaminergic neurons (Busch et al., 2009; Busch and Tanimoto, 2010).
evidence: Supported by comparison with cited literature (Busch et al., 2009; Busch and Tanimoto, 2010).

claim: Sleep loss through activation of octopaminergic neurons does not result in rebound sleep.
source: In addition, previous findings showed that sleep loss through activation of octopaminergic neurons does not result in rebound sleep (Seidner et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by citation to Seidner et al., 2015.

claim: Light inhibits the wake-promoting effects of octopamine.
source: and light inhibits the wake-promoting effects of octopamine (Shang et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to Shang et al., 2011.

claim: All MS1 neurons in the SOG are octopaminergic.
source: We found that all MS1 neurons in the SOG are octopaminergic (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Co-expression of Gal80 in TDC2 neurons removed all MS1-Gal4 activity in the SOG.
source: Consistent with this finding, co-expression of Gal80, an inhibitor of Gal4, in TDC2 neurons removed all MS1-Gal4 activity in the SOG (Figure 4D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Activation of non-TDC2 MS1 neurons did not alter sleep in males.
source: Indeed, we found that activation of non-TDC2 MS1 neurons did not alter sleep in males (Figure 4E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: Mutations in Tyramine β-hydroxylase (Tbh) prevented the male sleep loss induced by activation of MS1 neurons.
source: Furthermore, mutations in Tyramine β-hydroxylase (Tbh), another protein involved in octopamine synthesis (Monastirioti et al., 1996), and OAMB, an octopamine receptor implicated in sleep regulation (Crocker et al., 2010), prevented the male sleep loss induced by activation of MS1 neurons (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: Mutations in OAMB prevented the male sleep loss induced by activation of MS1 neurons.
source: Furthermore, mutations in Tyramine β-hydroxylase (Tbh), another protein involved in octopamine synthesis (Monastirioti et al., 1996), and OAMB, an octopamine receptor implicated in sleep regulation (Crocker et al., 2010), prevented the male sleep loss induced by activation of MS1 neurons (Figure 4F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4F.

claim: A small number of octopaminergic neurons in the SOG mediate male-specific arousal through the OAMB receptor.
source: These data show that a small number of octopaminergic neurons in the SOG mediate male-specific arousal through the OAMB receptor.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of genetic manipulations.

claim: MS1 neurons do not express FRU.
source: We did not detect any overlap between the MS1 and FRU populations (Figure 5A,B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A,B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: MS1 neurons do not express DOUBLESEX (DSX).
source: nor did we detect DOUBLESEX (DSX), another transcription factor important for male sexual behavior, in MS1 neurons (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: A group of FRU neurons is in close proximity to the MS1 neurons in the SOG.
source: Interestingly, we observed a group of FRU neurons in close proximity to the MS1 neurons in the SOG (Figure 5B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Punctate reconstituted GFP (GRASP) signals in the region surrounding the esophagus were more pronounced in male brains compared with female brains.
source: We observed that punctate reconstituted GFP (i.e., GRASP) signals in the region surrounding the esophagus were more pronounced in male brains compared with female brains (Figure 5D,E).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D,E.

claim: GRASP signals were not observed in control flies.
source: GRASP signals were not observed in control flies, which demonstrates that the observed GRASP signals are not due to leaky transgene expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: There is sexual dimorphism in the potential contacts between MS1 and FRU neurons.
source: These data demonstrate sexual dimorphism in the potential contacts between MS1 and FRU neurons, which may account for the male-specific effects on sleep with activation of MS1 neurons.
evidence: Inferred from the GRASP experiment results.

claim: The NSYB pre-synaptic marker was observed in multiple brain areas known to be involved in male reproductive behavior when targeted to the octopamingeric subset of MS1 neurons.
source: When the NSYB pre-synaptic marker was targeted to the octopamingeric subset of MS1 neurons, we observed expression in multiple brain areas known to be involved in male reproductive behavior (Yamamoto and Koganezawa, 2013; Zhang et al., 2016), including the antennal lobe, lateral horn, lateral protocerebrum, anterior superior medial protocerebrum, and mushroom body regions (Figure 5F).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: MS1 neurons may make synaptic contacts with several clusters of FRU neurons that were not detected by the GRASP technique.
source: Since FRU neurons also send projections to these regions, it is possible that MS1 neurons make synaptic contacts with several clusters of FRU neurons that were not detected by the GRASP technique.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the overlap of projection patterns.

claim: The DSCAM post-synaptic marker was enriched around the esophagus.
source: In contrast to the pre-synaptic marker, the DSCAM post-synaptic marker was enriched around the esophagus (Figure 5G)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5G.

claim: MS1 neurons receive input from the FRU circuit through the region surrounding the esophagus.
source: where we observed strong GRASP signals, suggesting that MS1 neurons receive input from the FRU circuit through this region
evidence: Inferred from the co-localization of GRASP signals and DSCAM marker.

claim: The NSYB pre-synaptic marker was also observed in the region surrounding the esophagus.
source: However, the NSYB pre-synaptic marker was also observed in the region surrounding the esophagus (Figure 5F)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Octopaminergic MS1 neurons are positioned to receive and send information through the region surrounding the esophagus.
source: indicating octopaminergic MS1 neurons are positioned to receive and send information through this region of the brain
evidence: Inferred from the presence of both pre- and post-synaptic markers in the same region.

claim: Upon application of ATP, a number of FRU neurons exhibited a marked increase in the GCaMP6m signal.
source: Upon application of ATP, a number of FRU neurons exhibited a marked increase in the GCaMP6m signal (Figure 6A,B)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: MS1 neurons act upstream of several FRU clusters.
source: indicating that MS1 neurons act upstream of several FRU clusters
evidence: Inferred from the calcium imaging results.

claim: One of the FRU clusters that responded to MS1 stimulation appeared to be P1 interneurons in the posterior brain.
source: Based on the position of their cell bodies, one of these clusters appeared to be P1 interneurons in the posterior brain.
evidence: Inferred from the anatomical position of the responding neurons.

claim: MS1 neurons provide excitatory input to P1 neurons.
source: Using the more restricted R71G01-LexA driver, we confirmed an excitatory input from MS1 to P1 neurons (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: One bilateral FRU cluster located above the antennal lobes is likely to be mAL.
source: One of these bilateral FRU cluster located above the antennal lobes is likely to be mAL, which provides inhibitory input to P1 neurons (Clowney et al., 2015; Kallman et al., 2015).
evidence: Inferred from anatomical position and cited literature (Clowney et al., 2015; Kallman et al., 2015).

claim: A neuronal pair in the superior protocerebrum may be FRU-expressing dopaminergic aSP4 neurons.
source: In addition, although we could not confirm their identity, a neuronal pair in the superior protocerebrum may be FRU-expressing dopaminergic aSP4 neurons (Figure 6A)
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on anatomical position.

claim: The activity of aSP4 neurons has been shown to reflect mating drive.
source: whose activity has recently been shown to reflect mating drive (Zhang et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2016.

claim: Stimulation of MS1 neurons led to strong calcium responses in males but not in females in mAL neurons and the arch neuropil region.
source: Quantification of the GCaMP6m signal in the cell bodies of mAL neurons as well as the arch neuropil region heavily innervated by FRU neurons showed that stimulation of MS1 neurons led to strong calcium responses in males but not in females (Figure 6B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: P1 neurons are not present in females.
source: Since P1 neurons are not present in females, excitatory input from MS1 to P1 is also male specific.
evidence: Draws from established knowledge about P1 neurons.

claim: Excitatory input from MS1 to P1 is male specific.
source: Since P1 neurons are not present in females, excitatory input from MS1 to P1 is also male specific.
evidence: Inferred from the absence of P1 neurons in females.

claim: MS1 neurons provide broad excitatory input to the FRU circuit.
source: Additional unidentified FRU clusters responded strongly to activation of MS1 neurons, indicating that MS1 neurons provide broad excitatory input to the FRU circuit.
evidence: Inferred from the calcium imaging results showing multiple responding FRU clusters.

claim: Activation of MS1 neurons in a fru mutant background had little effect on male sleep.
source: Consistent with the idea that MS1 neurons act upstream of FRU neurons, we found that activation of MS1 neurons in a fru mutant background had little effect on male sleep (Figure 7A).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: MS1 activation in a dsx mutant background produced little effect on male sleep.
source: In addition, MS1 activation in a dsx mutant background produced little effect on male sleep (Figure 7A)
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: MS1 neurons act upstream of dsx-expressing neurons.
source: suggesting that MS1 neurons also act upstream of dsx-expressing neurons
evidence: Inferred from the dsx mutant experiment results.

claim: P1 neurons express both FRU and DSX.
source: P1 neurons express both FRU and DSX (Kimura et al., 2008)
evidence: Supported by citation to Kimura et al., 2008.

claim: P1 neurons exhibit calcium responses to MS1 stimulation.
source: and our data show that they exhibit calcium responses to MS1 stimulation
evidence: Supported by experimental data from calcium imaging.

claim: P1 neurons are a prime candidate for a FRU cluster acting downstream of MS1 neurons to promote wakefulness.
source: and thus are a prime candidate for a FRU cluster acting downstream of MS1 neurons to promote wakefulness
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of calcium imaging and genetic experiments.

claim: Activation of P1 neurons using a highly restricted P1-split-Gal4 driver resulted in a strong reduction in male sleep, but had no effect on female sleep.
source: Indeed, activation of P1 neurons using a highly restricted P1-split-Gal4 driver (Inagaki et al., 2014) resulted in a strong reduction in male sleep, but had no effect on female sleep as expected from the sexually dimorphic nature of P1 (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Artificial activation of P1 has been shown to trigger courtship behaviors in isolated males.
source: Artificial activation of P1 has been shown to trigger courtship behaviors in isolated males (Kohatsu et al., 2011; von Philipsborn et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to Kohatsu et al., 2011; von Philipsborn et al., 2011.

claim: Wing extension in males with activated P1 neurons was observed.
source: and similarly we observed wing extension in males with activated P1 neurons (Video 3)
evidence: Supported by video observations (Video 3).

claim: Wing extension did not last beyond the first hour of thermogenetic activation of P1 neurons.
source: However, wing extension did not last beyond the first hour of thermogenetic activation of P1 neurons
evidence: Supported by experimental observations.

claim: Continued activation of P1 neurons led to behavior typical of awake flies such as pacing, feeding, and grooming.
source: and continued activation led to behavior typical of awake flies such as pacing, feeding, and grooming (Video 4)
evidence: Supported by video observations (Video 4).

claim: MS1 activation did not produce wing extension at any time.
source: In contrast, MS1 activation did not produce wing extension at any time (Videos 2–4)
evidence: Supported by video observations (Videos 2–4).

claim: Activation of P1 via MS1 is not strong enough to trigger courtship behavior.
source: perhaps because activation of P1 via MS1 is not strong enough to trigger courtship behavior
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the observation that MS1 activation does not produce wing extension.

claim: MS1 neurons affect mating success indirectly by providing octopamingeric arousal input to the courtship circuit.
source: Our data suggest MS1 neurons affect mating success indirectly by providing octopamingeric arousal input to the courtship circuit.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of behavioral and circuit analysis.

claim: When FRU neurons were activated using P2X2 and ATP, MS1 neurons in the SOG exhibited an increased GCaMP6m signal in a male-specific fashion.
source: Indeed, we found that when we used P2X2 and ATP to active the FRU circuit, MS1 neurons in the SOG exhibited an increased GCaMP6m signal in a male-specific fashion (Figure 7C,D).
evidence: Supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C,D.

claim: MS1 neurons did not detect calcium responses when P1 neurons were stimulated using R71G01-LexA.
source: We did not detect calcium responses in MS1 neurons when we stimulated P1 neurons using R71G01-LexA (max △F/F0 = 0.01 ± 0.01)
evidence: Supported by experimental data from calcium imaging.

claim: MS1 and P1 neurons do not form a positive feedback loop.
source: which suggests that MS1 and P1 neurons do not form a positive feedback loop
evidence: Inferred from the lack of calcium responses in MS1 neurons when P1 neurons were stimulated.

claim: FRU neurons other than the P1 cluster act upstream of MS1 neurons.
source: and FRU neurons other than the P1 cluster act upstream of MS1 neurons
evidence: Inferred from the observation that FRU circuit activation elicits MS1 responses but P1 activation does not.

claim: MS1 neurons receive input from FRU neurons and send excitatory input to several FRU clusters to balance sleep and sexual behaviors specifically in male flies.
source: Collectively, our data show that MS1 neurons receive input from FRU neurons and, in turn, send excitatory input to several FRU clusters to balance sleep and sexual behaviors specifically in male flies.
evidence: Inferred from the combined results of calcium imaging experiments showing bidirectional connectivity.

claim: Male flies suppressed sleep in the presence of females.
source: We found that male flies suppressed sleep in the presence of females
evidence: Supported by experimental data from sleep assays.

claim: Sexual satiety attenuated female-induced male sleep suppression.
source: and that sexual satiety or elevated levels of sleep drive attenuated female-induced male sleep suppression
evidence: Supported by experimental data from satiety experiments.

claim: Elevated levels of sleep drive attenuated female-induced male sleep suppression.
source: and that sexual satiety or elevated levels of sleep drive attenuated female-induced male sleep suppression
evidence: Supported by experimental data from sleep deprivation experiments.

claim: Sleep and sex drives compete to control behavior.
source: These findings demonstrate that sleep and sex drives compete to control behavior
